speechtext:
If my right hon. friend insists, I can tell him that it is that notary who was brought into the county, and who was the leading man in the county of Richmond. My right hon. friend knows him perfectly well. He came there and made that statement.
And further on:

maintopic: ADDRESS IN ANSWER TO HIS EXCELLENCY'S SPEECH.
speechtext:
I would like to state to my right hon. friend that the name of that notary is Begin, a well-known political worker.
And on November 22 the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) read a declaration in this House signed by Paul Emile Lamarche, a Conservative who had taken part in the meeting referred to in the township of King-sey, in the county of Drummond. I do not see anything in that declaration to substantiate the charge that the words referred to by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) were used by Notary Begin-who, by the way, is not from Richmond, but from Windsor Mills. Mr. Begin, having seen the report in the Montreal ' Gazette ' of the discussion in this House, wired me the following:
Windsor Mills, Que., Nov. 22.
E. W. Tobin,
House of Commons,
Ottawa.
Montreal ' Gazette ' reports Mr. Monk asserts I declared during campaign that if necessary the Canadian navy could be used to pound England. Please deny. I never said that nor anything like it. Assertion as absurd as idea. Am writing open letter of denial to Mr. Monk through ' Gazette.' If they publish can produce declarations to prove my denial if assertion persisted in.
Joseph Vide;., J.P.

Smith, of Kingsey Falls, makes the same declaration, signed before Joseph Vidal. J.P. And Mr. J. B. Prefontaine, of Kingsey Falls, formerly of South Durham, who is a brother of a good Conservative, Dr. Prefontaine, of South Durham, who is known to the hon. member for Jacques Cartier, and was with him in the county of Drummond and canvassed the French electors of that township of Durham the Saturday before the polling took place, makes a declaration in the same form as the others.
I would ask the hon. member for Jacques Cartier to withdraw his words in reference to Mr. Begin, especially as I see that the declaration that he got from his own party, Mr. Lamarche, a Conservative of Montreal, did not substantiate in any way the statement that the words attributed to my friend, Mr. Begin, of Windsor Mills, had been utered by that gentleman.

I thought perhaps my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) would like to take the opportunity to speak. I would be glad to afford him the opportunity to say anything he desires. Mr. Speaker, we have listened with considerable interest, and, I must confess for myself with a little endurance to the magnificent address made by the hon. member for East Hastings (Mr. Northrup). But I think the House generally will agree with me that that hon. gentleman travelled from Dan to Beersheba in that address. There is no question in the King's speech, or outside of it that he did not refer to. Even questions upon which he has made speeches in this House repeatedly for the last four or five years he thought fit to bring up again to the attention of parliament at this time. He began by saying that the Liberal party in Canada was under the tyranny of a despot.

Well, I am a democrat myself, but I have no objection to the despot if he is a good one. The chief objection to the despot and tyrant is the unreasonable way in which they administer power. But when a man in power can lead the public forces of this country to a considerable measure, at any rate, of national success, as has been done by the leader of this government, I think we can excuse him if he exercises considerable personal authority over those who follow him. So far as I am concerned, I suppose the hon. gentleman will place me in the category iof a sl,ave, 'as he would other members on this side. Well, I am no man's slave and no man's tool. Although I have taken the position in this House on almost every occasion since I came here, of supporting the policy of the leader of this House (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), I have done so after having given my very best judgment on the conditions and circumstances and arrived at an independent conclusion that this was best for this country.
My hon. friend from Hastings (Mr. Northrup), made some reference to the general trade of Canada. His remarks were perfectly in keeping with what I think are his well-trained Tory instincts. I do not blame my hon. friend for anything he says of that character because if there is one man in the opposition who is true to Tory record and that is possessed of real Tory instincts, who has a Tory disposition and who always arrives, perhaps in a roundabout way, at Tory conclusions, it is my hon. friend from Hastings (Mr. Northrup). I was, however, surprised that there is one man in this House who would complain about the improvement and increase in the general trade of this country. That Sir, is the basis of the prosperity of every country, that is the basis of the prosperity of this country. The evidence of the progress and development of the trade of Canada is the evidence of our national prosperity. The greatest countries in the universe to-day are France, England, Germany and the United States. They are the four great nations of the world. I am glad, to say that as a member of this House I have no regrets on that score, but will always contribute my influence and vote in favour of increasing the trade of this country. My hon. friend made some reference to the naval question, and in my opinion touched every part of it except that part of it which is before the House for consideration, and I must say for I followed my hon. friend very closely last session, that he, with the same expedition as the rest of his party, has made a wonderful change in his position in regard to that question. My hon. friend shakes his head. I make that statement and I will give my hon. friend the proof. What was his position on the navy Mr. RALPH SMITH.
last session? It was that this country and this parliament had no jurisdiction to pass a Bill of that kind and he began and argued and ended the speech by making a plea to the Prime Minister of this country to submit the question of the authority for the establishment of the navy in Canada to the Supreme Court of Canada. That was the position taken by my hon. friend at that time.
Hear, hear.

It is very remarkable that my hon. friend did not mention the Supreme Court to-day. Not only so but he has accepted fully the position taken by the leader of the opposition this session against the construction of a Canadian navy and has emphasized the necessity for a contribution to Great Britain at this date when his own leader is convinced that whatever crisis might have existed a year ago none exists to-day, and has eliminated from his proposals any question of a contribution to Great Britain.
I wish to follow some of the remarks of my hon. friend from Yale-Cariboo (Mr. Burrell), a representative from the province of British Columbia. The complaint I have to make of his speech is that it was prepared as a defence against the Borden policy of last year and therefore could not fit in with the Borden policy of this year. It was quite evident to me before my hon. friend had gone far, that there was very little in common between the criticism he was making against the policy announced by his leader at this session, and his position taken with regard to the policy announced by the leader last session. I notice however, that he still clings to the old flag. He did it of course, with a considerable amount of brag, with some amount of dramatic description. He showed great deference to the empire and he had a great wealth of patriotic phrasing, but it is easy to see that these are not the materials that build ships for the navy. The patriotism of language and fine words will not strengthen the British Empire. The professions of hon. gentlemen as to their loyalty make no contribution to the progress to the increased stability of this country or to its protection or development. We live in deeds, not words, and my hon. friend can talk until doomsday, but if that is all he has to offer as a contribution to the development of this great country, then surely we have failed in the great mission and responsibility which rest on us.
My hon. friend is at variance with his own leader in the province of British Columbia. A great deal has been said recently, and said by ministers in the local government, as to the probability of my good friend Mr. McBride coming down to take charge of the political destinies of the Con-

servative party in Ottawa. If my hon. friend has been looking over the press of British Columbia, he must have arrived at the conclusion that some of the strongest leaders of his party have decided that the principle of a Canadian navy enunciated and inaugurated by the Laurier government is the 'right principle. I would remind the hon. gentleman that just a few days ago the president of the Privy Council of the McBride government, at a military banquet in Victoria, announced himself absolutely and emphatically in favour of the policy of the Laurier government in regard to a Canadian navy. I would remind my hon. friend also that to-day Captain Clive Phillips Woolley, an old opponent of mine, a straight-forward, outspoken, independent gentleman, the president of the Navy League in British Columbia, has been lecturing through the country and in the city of Toronto. What does he say, one of the leaders of the Conservative party in British Columbia, president of the Navy League, paid perhaps by the Navy League to go through the country and discuss the question of a Canadian navy? He said: I am in absolute agreement with the principle of a Canadian navy as proposed by the Laurier government. It is perfectly true- I have no disposition to deceive the House -that Mr. Woolley has said: I would have been better pleased if the Prime Minister and his government had gone further, and had made a contribution. I believe there has been a crisis in England for some time, I believe there is a crisis still and I would have been in absolute accord with the Liberal party if they had provided for a contingency of that description. That is the position that Mr. Woolley takes and is what he said. When members from the Dominion parliament go back to the capital city of Victoria or the cities of British Columbia and designate the Canadian navy as a tin-pot navy, I want to put myself on record as saying that I have absolutely no use or tolerance for a man of that description. When he takes that position he is slapping directly at my hon. friend who is not in his seat, the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Barnard) who, when he went back to the city of Victoria last session, designated the Canadian navy as a tin-pot navy. But now, I said that the premier of British Columbia was at variance with my hon. friend. Of course, Mr. McBride spoke before the hon. leader of the opposition moved his amendment, but that would only indicate that my good friend, the leader of 'the opposition, had not taken his friend, Mr. McBride, into bis confidence. I think that is a very unfair advantage to take. When you are compelled to agree on points ultimately, whether you disagree at the present time, it is only fair that you should know what
is in the future. The training ship, ' Rainbow/ went into the harbour of Esquimalt in my district the other day. My hon. friend the Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Templeman) was present. My hon. friend the member for Victoria was present and my hon. friend-and I may call him so because he is my friend-the premier of the province of British Columbia was present. I want to read to the hon. member for Yale-Cariboo (Mr. Burrell), and to the Conservatives of this House and to eastern Canada, what Mr. McBride, at the official reception of the ' Rainbow/ said about the Canadian navy. I can only say that if the prognostications of some of the responsible ministers of British Columbia, who anticipate that Mr. McBride is going to take charge of the destinies of the Conservative party happen to come true before -these hon. gentlemen have had an opportunity of changing again, then Mr. McBride will support the Laurier government on the question of the Canadian navy. Mr. McBride said:
He entirely endorsed what Mr. Templeman had so eloquently said and what his honoured leader of the government has been pleased to say also.
I want to call my hon. friend's attention particularly to this report.
We realize the great significance of the step the Canadian people have taken in the establishing of the Canadian navy

Is there any misgiving about that?
-into which the Canadian people have entered with all heartiness

Now the theory of hon. gentlemen opposite that the Canadian people know nothing about it and that in order to give them an opportunity to know something about it my hon. friend should dissolve this parliament and go back to the country is altogether at variance with what Mr. McBride says that they have entered into it with all heartiness

-and with every determination that at all costs we shall take a place in the defence of the empire such as the energy of our people in numbers and wealth would warrant us in doing.
Hear, hear.
We have the support of the hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton (Mr. Hughes). I am surprised that we did not have it when he made his speech.
I was commending the expression of the Prime Minister of British Columbia that we should support and not disintegrate the empire.

My hon. friend says that he was commending the speech

of the premier of British Columbia that we should support the empire.
Yes.

The premier says that to support the empire we must have a Canadian navy and that is just the difference between my hon. friend and the premier of British Columbia. The hon. member for Yale-Cariboo thinks we should support the empire, but he thinks we can do it with fine phrases. The hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton thinks we can support the empire but he does not think it is necessary to spend money to do so. I have made no preparation to say anything with reference to the hon. gentleman, he has provoked what I have been saying, but I noticed that when my hon. friend made his speech recently he did not say one single word in defence of the amendment of the leader of the opposition. The only reference he made to that amendment was when he was taking his seat and when he said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to say that I am willing to support the amendment of my honoured leader.
Now, I want to come to the consideration of the position taken by the leader of the opposition generally and I want to bring, if I can, the attention of these gentlemen back to the position that if there was any mistake made in the formation of the Canadian navy, if there was any mistake made in spending the money of the people of this country in connection with that navy, if there was any mistake about the policy that this government has provided for and is carrying out, the responsibility belongs to every member of this House. The House must have been struck by this fact that in the whole discussion on this question hon. gentlemen have never referred to the session of 1909, and that is the beginning of the whole thing. I listened to the magnificent speech made by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) on that occasion, and to the resolution with which he concluded. I have read it again. I listened to the speech of the leader of the opposition that backed up that speech of the hon. member for North Toronto and the resolution and I have read it again, and I want to make this statement that everything in those speeches, everything in the position taken at that time, justifies this government and the country in what they are doing in connection with the Canadian navy. I will say the opposite, that nothing in the speech of my hon. friend from North Toronto and nothing in the speech of the leader of the opposition bears any relation whatever to the proposals that these hon. gentlemen have made in 1910 or at the present session. Now, Sir, the responsibility for a project of this kind was when we commenced it, and what are the facts? The resolution was proposed, the resolution was submitted to Mr. RALPH SMITH.
this House, the leader of the opposition amended that resolution to make it unanimous and responsible ministers went to England on the authority of that resolution. These ministers went to England and declared to the British authorities that the policy of Canada was for a navy in Canada which would defend the right, the trade and the position of Canada and would at the same time be a contribution towards the defence of the empire. Who gave them that mandate? Every responsible member of parliament, in the session of 1909. Assuming, therefore, that the whole proposal is unreasonable, assuming for the moment, as these hon. gentlemen say that there is no necessity for a Canadian navy, what I contend is that every hon. member of this House is under obligation, if he is a straightforward man, to say:	1
was a partner in the creation of that proposal. Horvever much hon. gentlemen opposite may refuse to take the responsibility of their action in 1909; however much they may hide their heads in the sand; they are face to face with the records of parliament, and the conclusion of the intelligent people of the country must be that parliament in 1909 unanimously decided to establish a Canadian navy for Canadian interests and for the interests of the empire. There is nothing like going back to the law and the testimony, and no matter how much hon. gentlemen opposite may try to shelve this responsibility, the responsibility rests upon them and will always rest on them. Let me ask hon. gentlemen opposite how they can explain the remarks made by the leader of the opposition in 1909, when they attempted to avoid responsibility for whatever has happened since then in connection with the naval policy. I ask these hon. gentlemen opposite how they can brush aside the words of the leader of the opposition spoken in the House on March 19, 1909, when he said:
In so far as my right hon. friend the Prime Minister to-day outlined the lines of naval defence of this country I am entirely at one with him. I am entirely of opinion, in the first place, that the proper line upon which we should proceed in that regard is the line of having a Canadian naval force of our own.
Mark that. Can there be any dispute about these words? Can it be denied that that being the date at which this important policy was founded, that the leader of the opposition assisted at the foundation. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden) is a gentleman for -whom I have the highest respect, but I must say that in my opinion no parallel can be found in the political history of this country for such a quick change of attitude on a public question, by a gentleman who assumes the responsibility of leader of a great party. Mr. R. L. Borden continued to say:-

The other experiment has been tried as between Australia and the mother country and it has not worked satisfactorily in any respect; so, I am at one with the Prime Minister as far as this is concerned. I am at one with him in this respect also.
I want hon. gentlemen opposite to listen to this:-
I am at one with him in this respect also that I think that an expenditure of money designed for that purpose ought, in the main at least, to be under the control of our own parliament.
Why, Sir, when we take his present proposition for an imperial navy, which must be controlled by the imperial authorities, and contrast it with the position he took when he spoke the language I have cited to the House, we can easily see where he is at. He said further:-
And that by making an appropriation of that kind and attending to the defence of our own coasts, by co-operation and co-ordination with the imperial naval forces, we would be doing our duty not only to Canada but to the empire as a whole.
Is it any wonder, in view of this language, that I should say that the leader of the opposition must take the responsibility for assisting, in the year 1909, in the foundation of the naval policy of the government? I say, further, that every position taken by the leader of the opposition since that date, when the project of a Canadian navy was founded, is contrary to the proposition which he laid down in the year 1909. Listen to what the hon. the leader of the opposition has since proposed. Last session his proposition was, in the first place, that the whole question of a Canadian navy ought to be submitted to the people, and in the second place, that an immediate contribution ought to be made to the mother land to provide assistance in what he considered to be a period of crisis. The position taken by the leader of the opposition to-day is an extension of the position taken last year. He now says that the whole question should be submitted to the people, and the crisis not existing to-day, the question of a contribution is absolutely eliminated from his plan. I say, therefore, and I say it without fear of contradiction, that the policy supported by the leader of the opposition in 1909 has been absolutely and entirely carried out by the government at the present day, and every position taken by him since then upon which he has tested the opinion of this House is contrary to the doctrine he laid down in 1909. I am a democrat, I have been trained in that school and I am not ashamed of it; I have always tried to act with caution and to devote the greatest possible investigation into every project before I assume responsibility for it; I can quite conceive that there might be occasions in this country, as there may be in any country, when great national projects might, with propriety, be submitted to the people, but, if the people ought to decide as to the navy I tell the leader of the opposition that they ought to have decided it in 1909, when the leader of the opposition moved his original resolution in this House, and not in 1910. In all his utterances in 1909, was there a single word said in favour of submitting this question to the people? Was there a single gentleman on the other side of the House who then ventured to suggest that the proposition should be submitted to the people? No, Sir, not one single reference was ever made in that whole debate to the people of Canada being given an opportunity to consider this question before we entered on the project. I wonder if gentlemen opposite from the province of Quebec presented this question to the electors of Drummond-Arthabaska in its true light? I wonder if they told them that the Canadian navy was reaily established in 1909, and that not one member in the House said a single word at that time in favour of referring the question to the people? And,' suppose we adopted the principle of a referendum in this country, where would we draw the line? Everything that comes before this parliament is in a sense important, and what would we refer to the people and what would we not refer to them? There is only a question of degree between a thing that costs the most and a thing that costs the least. One thing may cost $1,000,000 and another may cost only $1, but the $1 belongs to the people just as much as the one million does. I say to hon. gentlemen opposite, and I have no doubt they know it, that their proposition in regard to the general question of referring these matters to the people is utterly impracticable and utterly impossible. We are representatives in this House, not delegates. I can conceive of small nations which might carry on their business by sending delegates to a conference instead of sending representatives to parliament ; but if the people are to decide matters directly, and not through their representatives, then black balls and white balls would accomplish the business just as effectively as representatives in parliament. The representation of the people of this country in parliament involves a very heavy expenditure, and if the members of this parliament are not to think out public questions according to the conditions and circumstances surrounding them, then I submit there is really no necessity for representatives at all. One would suppose, to hear hon. gentlemen opposite talking of this as a great principle, that it was a feature of the policy of the Conservative party. Though not a native Canadian, I have studied the political history of this country, and I would

ask the hon. member for Yale-Cariboo (Mr. Burrell) how often did the Conservative government of this country since confederation submit questions to the decision of the people? How often did they dissolve parliament in order to obtain the decision of the people on any project before carrying it through? The hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) did specify certain questions which he thought might very properly be brought under this principle, for instance, the autonomy of the Northwest provinces. My hon. friend from East Grey is not in his place, but I was going to ask him this question. The Conservative government of this country took the responsibility of bringing the crown colony of British Columbia into the confederation. There is no comparison in importance between that project and ajn extension of the autonomy of western provinces which have always been part of the Dominion ; and yet did the Conservative government submit a referendum on the question of bringing British Columbia into the confederation? I do not say that I would have supported a proposal of that kind if I had been a member of this House at the time. I am merely putting that ease before the House in contrast to the suggestion of the hon. member for East Grey. In the discussion of that question in 1872, as the records show, three amendments were proposed to the terms of union. Those amendments were not in favour of giving the people a voice in the decision of the matter, but were in favour of giving the members of this House at that time an opportunity of ascertaining what view the people of eastern Canada took of those terms, and every one of those three amendments was voted down by the Conservative party in this House. Was there any plebiscite taken in this country when we undertook the responsibility of forming a militia? This government has increased the expenditure for that service up to nearly $7,000,000 a year, a very much larger sum than the Canadian navy will cost for some years to come. Has there ever been any suggestion made by hon. gentlemen opposite that the question of enlarging the militia should be submitted to the people before that was done? What is the navy, after all? It is simply an extension of the principle of national protection, and if that is right in one direction, it ought to be right in another. I submit that with this great country developing at the rate it is, with national issues of great importance constantly arising at short notice in this parliament, the proposition submitted by our hon. friends opposite becomes absolutely impossible. Let me come to the present position of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition. He has changed his position again. He has disposed of the Mr. RALPH SMITH.
question of providing for any urgency or crisis in the old land. vVas there a crisis a year ago? Was there ever a crisis, with regard to the relations of Great Britain and Germany. There was a crisis in the mind of Robert Blatchford ; there was a crisis in the pages of the yellow journals ; but every intelligent precaution was taken by the responsible ministers in England, especially in the last two or three years, and it was impossible to find in the midst of the political conflict there in the last twelve months, a single reference to any crisis with regard to Germany to necessitate any special consideration either a year ago or at the present time.
My hon. friend from Yale and Cariboo (Mr. Burrell) quoted from a speech of Lord Rosebery to prove his position. But what was the date of that speech? It was the very date when the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) was so seriously impressed by the seriousness of the crisis that he brought into this House his famous resolution. In that year, the year 1909, I admit that there was a great deal of feeling and excitement in the old country, but I have had considerable experience in that country. I was 34 years of age when I came to Canada, and I had previously some little experience in English politics, and I have no hesitation in stating that the war scare of a year ago was just the ordinary one that has frequently been raised to suit political times and conditions. Was there an emergency a year ago? My hon. friend must have thought so since he wanted Canada to make a contribution to the naval defence of the empire. Is there an emergency to-day? My hon. friend from Hastings (Mr. Northrup) says there is and so does my hon. friend from Yale-Cariboo (Mr. Burrell), yet they both propose to support an amendment that makes no provision to meet that emergency. I have asked was there an emergency last year. I did not believe so, and I voted against any provision from this country to meet an imaginary contingency. But if there was a real and substantial crisis a year ago, what is the condition to-day? My hon. friend the leader oi the opposition argued that we should have had an investigation to find that out. In his last proposal he puts himself in the position of the Prime Minister and points out what he and his party would do if they were in power. They would, he said, correspond with the government of the old country, they would find out by investigation and inquiry whether any imminent danger realty existed, and if they discovered that such did exist they would come back to parliament and ask for the necessary means to meet the crisis. Well, if the hon. gentleman admits that there is a crisis-as hon. members opposite have done in their speeches-why does he

not make provision to meet it this year as he did last? Is he going to let it go by default? He has had now, since we last met, a good many months' opportunity to investigate, and surely he Is a wiser man to-day than he was a year ago. In his capacity as leader of the opposition, the hon. gentleman is saddled with responsibility from which he cannot escape. He has said what he would do were he leader of the government. But he is the leader of a great party, which is also bound to do what it can to protect the institutions of the country, and he is just as responsible for the education of public opinion as he would be if he were Prime Minister. But up to the present he has made no such investigation, and the result is that he does not know if there really exists any crisis or emergency which call for action on the part of Canada and submits to this House a resolution which is remarkable for nothing so much as its indefiniteness.
Then he takes the position that the Canadian navy should not be a separate unit, but should be under one central control, that of the British Admiralty. But that is in direct contradiction of the position taken by him in 1909. In his speech of March 29, 1909, he said:
I am entirely of opinion in the first place that the proper line upon which we should proceed in that regard is the line of having a Canadian naval force of our own. I entirely believe in that. The other experiment has been tried as between Australia and the mother country and it has not worked satisfactorily in any respect. In Great Britain the contribution has perhaps been regarded as rather unsatisfactory. In Australia it failed in the end to meet with the approval of the people for the reason that Great Britain felt restrained to ask Australia that the field of operations of the squadron should be extended to the China and Indian seas, and when the operations of that squadron were so extended the Australians felt that the contribution which they had been making for some years past was not really being used to give that protection to Australia that her interest demanded.
So that the individual unit system my hon. friend then considered impossible. It was found impossible in Australia. But if it was impossible in Australia, what special conditions now exist which make it possible in this country?
In conclusion let me say that I believe the people of this country will remember a few things. The first is that the naval policy of this country was determined in 1909 upon the resolution presented by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) and supported by the leader of the opposition. That was the time when the Canadian navy was built. There may be of course objections to the Bill as brought down, and my hon. friends have a right to criticise its details. But what I say is this, that in 1909 they stood for the absolute principle of a Canadian navy, and a Canadian navy only. But in 1910 and this session they have taken up a position contradicting that. Such complete reversal of policy on a great question of this kind can never be acceptable to the people. My hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) pointed out to the possibility of the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) going to British Columbia. For mv part, I would be delighted to see him there, and he would have as far as I am concerned, just as good a reception as Dick McBride gave to the Prime Minister. But there is one question which the people of that province will put to him. They will ask him which of his three policies he stands for. They will say to him: You took the responsibility of building a navy in 1909, parliament adopted that policy on the terms of your own resolution and the strength of your own speeches, do you stand for it now? If he replies that the latest policy he advocated is the best, then the question will naturally be put to him: What guarantee have we that, if we should support you, you will not by the time you get into power, have adopted another policy. You have made a complete change of front within eighteen months, how do we know that we may not have our confidence betrayed again and be playing into the hands of political deceivers.
An hon. gentleman supporting the Conservative party took the responsibility of making a statement on the floor of the House to-day which I am not sure jwill meet with the support of the hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton (Mr. Hughes). He took the responsibility of saying that the whole of British Columbia, that the whole of the west was against the Laurier policy. Well, they will have to exempt Mr. McBride. We have demonstrated that to the House very clearly. They have to exempt the president of his council-that is perfectly true. They have to exempt Mr. Clive Phillips-Woolley, president of the Navy League, and a prominent Conservative of British Columbia. The hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton (Mr. Hughes) has been in British Columbia. What is the feeling in that province on this question. The feeling in British Columbia, and especially on the coast, is that if- there is any fault to be found with this policy, it is only that it does not go far enough. There is not a single man in British Columbia who has not taken the position that the principle of a Canadian navy, the principle of spending Canadian money on Canadian ships for the protection of Canadian trade and the training of Canadian sailors is right. As I have said, some of them want to go

further. But that is not the position for hon. members opposite to take, because they are opposed to the Canadian navy, and naturally, would be more opposed to it if it were larger. It is a good thing for them that it is as small as it is, since they do not want it, but wish to submit the question to the people: it is a good thing for them that this is a ' tin-pot navy ' and the expenditure on it is as small as it is. These hon. gentlemen have thrown to the winds anything which would serve them as an argument that they are not entirely opposed to the principle of a Canadian navy. And I do not understand why men should object to a Canadian navy who do not object also to the Canadian militia-the two things are the same as far as I can see, for each is a national system of protection and paid for out of the public treasury. But these hon. gentlemen have not made any complaint as to the militia, nor have they ever suggested the submission of the militia question to the people.
Now, the people of this country want something definite. I believe the people would rather vote for a man who sometimes makes a mistake, than vote for a man who does nothing. And the difference between the Liberal party and the opposition, judging the opposition by the amendment proposed by its leader, is the difference between a policy of doing something for the national development, and a policy of doing nothing. Of course, we have to admit that, in this, hon. gentlemen opposite are following the true traditions of Toryism. The one thing that makes these hon. gentlemen sore is the fact_ that the Laurier government has done things, that great national projects have been carried out and that the country has made progress under this government. I do not pretend that there may not be dispute with regard to the details of this naval policy. But every great national project put into effect by this government has developed the country, increased its influence and raised it in the estimation of our own people and of the world.
Now, let me say in conclusion, the real spirit of empire is to develop this country. 1 am an Englishman myself, and my family connections are in England. But I realize that Canada is part of the British Empire and that the more you do for Canada the more you benefit the empire. I submit that it is true of every great national project that the argument against it has been reduced by some thinkers to the contention that it would lead to independence or the contention that it would draw us away from the empire and into annexation with the United States. These have always been the cries raised by pessimistic souls in this country. Let any man look over the records of great national move-Mr. RALPH SMITH.
ments in Canada, from the Act of Confederation to the building of the Canadian navy, and he will see that the arguments raised by some people were simply these- that it would lead to independence or that it would lead to annexation. Sir, I do not believe any such arguments. This is part of the empire, and when we develop this part we are helping to develop the whole. This is part of the empire did I sav? Yes, and perhaps destined to be the great centre of the empire at some period in the world's history. If hon. gentlemen opposite would have the larger vision, if they would extend their political horizon, if they would have faith in the possibilities of this country including the possibility of its being the great centre of the British Empire, they would realize the importance of a policy of national development. 1 support the national policy that develops the interests of this country. But these hon. gentlemen tell us that to develop the national interest is dangerous. Sir, the foundations of British interests in this country are not in mere forms; they are not to be found only in words such as those used by the leader of the opposition. They are in sound principles of liberty and justice and the rights of man, under which every foreigner who becomes a subject in this part of the empire learns to prize our institutions and 'traditions against anything that he bears in recollection of his native land. The strength of the British Empire is in its traditions and institutions and from these it draws the power to assimilate new comers from other lands. There is no fear of the British Empire. Sir, the subterfuge of one who does not wish to do his duty is to clothe that unwillingness in extreme expressions of loyalty; the man who wants to do the least is always the man who professes a wish to do the most. That is a position that the people of this country will appreciate. It may be that this navy is at present a tin-pot navy ' as the hon. member for Victoria says. But if the hon. member thinks of it, he knows that the United States navy was a ' tin-pot navy only a decade ago. The mighty naval force of Japan was a * tin-pot navy at first. It is impossible to bring national institutions into existence in complete formlike men, they have to grow. Every great institution and reform has known its day of small things. We commence small; but we have commenced; and we stand or fall by this policy of a Canadian navy. I believe that the courage shown bv the government will be appreciated by the people; I believe the people will say: We will forgive mistakes in the men who do things, but we cannot forgive the political lethargy and indolence that never attempts to do anything.

Mr. Speaker, the House is now nearing the end of the first two weeks of the session. For the last ten days we have listened to a discussion on the subject which was the main topic of debate.last session. It would be futile on my part to speak at any length on the question of the navy. Even were I of a mind to do so, I gave my statement to the House last session in unequivocal terms and set forth what I took to be the wishes of the electors in the west riding of Huron. I have no knowledge or information which would lead me to believe that they have changed their opinion. In brief, I believe that four out of five, if they were asked their opinion, would vote against a regular navy, against old country militarism in any shape, or form, and I believe that if a vote was taken in my county that would be the result. The county, a portion of which I have the honour to represent, is principally Liberal. I have also been through the county of Dufferin and have asked a great many representative men there, almost to a man on the other side of politics, and I believe that their opinion is the same, that four out of five of them would vote against the imposition at this time, on this country of a regular navy.
The hon. gentleman who has just sat down, (Mr. Smith, Nanaimo), says: Why do you not object to the militia when you object to the navy? The militia has nothing to do with a regular, old country militarism. I am strongly in favour, and so are the people of my riding, of the militia. I would ask the government to back up the Minister of Militia in the desire he expresses for the improvement of the militia, but his hands are tied by a militia council. It is natural that gentlemen of the military profession should want to do things in their own way, but I would remark that in my younger days, when our expenditure on the militia was a million and a quarter instead of eight million dollars, we had in my own tovm three companies of militia who were out nearly once a week during the summer months. We now see nothing of them except once a year. A military inspector from the old land, a very estimable gentleman in his profession no doubt, but a man who wishes everything done in his own military way, has reported that we should have 15 more general officers at headquarters. If he puts that into effect then with the small number of militia we have in the country who go out to the few small camps that are held, we must be reminded of the disaster that recently almost came to a small South African republic when ten generals were rescued from death in one small merchant steamer. I stated last year that in my opinion, there was no crisis and I quoted the opinion of the greatest naval expert, Captain 14
Mahan, the author of ' Sea Power ' and other noted works. He expressed the belief that the great preparation of the German navy was in order to prevent the United States prohibiting German interference in South America, and when one thinks for a moment of what would happen if Germany should ever be so foolish as to go to war with England, it is seen that these preparations could not be against England. Thirty days after a declaration of war had been issued, a French army would be in Berlin and the Crowns are not so steady on the heads of European sovereigns that they would imperil them by the great danger of revolution which a war with England would entail. If there was such a war Germany would be a republic from that day evermore. We have had recent instances of revolutions and more are in the air. Reciprocity with the United States and other tariff matters have been the subjects of discussion. In a weekly report issued by one department of the government I see notices from Canadian agents in different countries, Mexico, Australia, the Netherlands, or some other distant place, that if Canadian merchants and manufacturers and farmers in certain lines will send to certain reputable merchants in these places, Canadians can do business. In the United States publications similar reports are published from American commercial agents in Owen Sound, Winnipeg, or Vancouver, or other Canadian places, informing the manufacturers, the merchants or the farmers of the United States that if they send to certain merchants in these Canadian centres they can do business. That is their purpose in this country. What have we to inform our farmers or merchants of ways and means by which they can further their business relations with our greatest trade competitors? May that not be one reason why they send four million dollars worth of goods into Canada against our $400,000 more or less to the United States? I do not object to a discussion of commercial relations with the United States because it would be discourteous and unbusinesslike not to carry on such discussions, but I ask on what the government found their information from the other man's point of view, whom have we in the United States to tell us their views, to furnish us with business information? I suggested last session that the first minister should appoint at the city of Washington a Canadian attache to advise in business matters the representative of the British Crown, who has our interests there at heart and who very very seldom knows anything about our affairs. I said that one of the former ministers of England, the Imperial Ambassador to Washington, had stated that seven-tenths of the business he had to do with the United States government was in connection with Can-



ada, and I now give notice that I shall at a future time, put a resolution on the order paper asking the government to appoint commercial agents in all the large centres of trade in the United States to give us information and to further the interests of Canadian manufacturers, farmers and tradesmen^ of all kinds. Remember the old legal maxim, a case well prepared is half won.
I am surprised that no reference is made in the speech from the Throne on the important subject of representation in this parliament. It has been current report in the newspapers that representatives of the maritime provinces will come to Ottawa to interview the government as to the representation of those provinces. I see nothing in the speech from the Throne with reference to that subject, but it is a matter which we should have discussed to the fullest extent. My own opinion, and I believe the opinion of the people whom I represent, is that we have too many representatives for this country in this parliament. I put it on this ground: I do not mean for one moment to argue the question of the pro rata, or system of representation.
I say we have too many representatives. If the apportionment between the provinces is the same as at confederation I have no objection to it, but there are too many. I wish to prove by a simple little illustration why it would be better to have a smaller representation. If you take the smaller municipalities in the county it will serve as an illustration. There are 25 municipalities in my own county, each having from five to seven representatives, or 130 representatives in all. Then, when we come to the county council we have one or two representatives for each municipality, or about fifty in all. On one occasion the Ross government tried to do away with that and to divide the county up into sixteen sections, but they did not succeed, and we went back to the old system of two representatives for each municipality. Then, when we come to the provincial legislature, we have three representatives for the county of Huron. That is, no doubt, proper; it has never been changed and no one objects to it, but the higher up we get the smaller the number. When we come to the Dominion parliament, the highest parliament in the land, we still have the same as for the provincial legislature. If the United States of America, with 90 millions of people, had the same number to represent them in proportion to the population that we have they would have 2,335 members of Congress. If the mother land, with 45 million people, had representatives to the same number as we have, or in the same proportion, they would have 1,452. I contend that if the British North America Act is to be changed with reference to the representation the number [DOT] Mr. LEWIS.
should be cut down. Our numbers will steadily increase until we have to change; let us do so now.
There is another matter that comes very close to every person in this country, and that is the cost of living. I contend that the question of the cost of living is one that-should receive our most earnest and careful consideration, because, no matter what explanation may be given as to the reason for it, there is no doubt of the fact that the crux of the matter is there is not enough food produced in the country to supply the demand. That is evidenced everywhere by the prices. The same thing is occurring on the other side of the line. I contend that we should limit our immigration and keep out all those of the non-producing classes who seek to enter our country. We should not have the stigma cast upon us that is cast upon the people on the other side of the line of having a nation of organ grinders and banana pedlars.
There is another matter with reference to which I wish to commend the government, and I am surprised that they have not gone farther in the same direction. I refer to their action with reference to the rules governing this House. The changes that they have made will be conducive to the best interests of the people, and I want to say, Sir, that the people are tired of this parliament sitting here for five, six ot eight months.
You are helping them to do it.

I w'as guilty once and only once, but I have nut been of late years. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Tolmie) and his leader will follow what I am going to tell them it will reduce the time of the session from one to two months. My suggestion has reference to the estimates. I submit thatl we should follow the rules that are carried! out in other countries which have been longer legislating than we have been. The mother land, Germany, France and and even the province of Ontario have rules with regard to the consideration of estimates different from those which prevail in this House. Four-fifths of the time of this House is taken up in the discussion of the estimates. I submit that without changing the rules of this House in so far as they affect the result we could reduce the length of the session by at least six weeks by a very slight change in our procedure. If the minister of any department will give notice that two weeks from a certain day he will be in Room 62, or>
whatever committee room it may be, with his estimates at a certain hour, say 10 a.nr., and let any hon. member in this' House be allowed to go there and investiJ gate the various items, it will be possible to pass all non-contentious items en bloc.

It would not affect the contentious items being brought up in this House. Ministers are generally urbane, amiable and kindly in their manner when they are passing their estimates, knowing nothing about the items themselves and being obliged to ask the engineer or official sitting near them and then passing the infor-, mation on to the committee. Why, Sir, I have known an item of $40,000 in this House to take up a whole sitting and items aggregating $10,000,000 to be passed in ten minutes without proper investigation. The time to stop a useless expenditure is not in the Public Accounts Committee after the money has been spent and when the matter is referred to a board of judges, i.e., a committee, the majority of whom are against any explanation. The time to stop it is before the expenditure is made. The government as a whole have the interest of the country at heart, and I believe they wish to prevent such unwarranted expenditures as we do. If they would simply have the estimates examined carefully by this mode and all non-contentious items passed en bloc a great improvement in the procedure would be effected. The opposition could appoint a committee to attend but any member of the House would be at liberty to ask any questions with regard to any item that he desired. Hours and hours of useful time of this country would be saved as well as thousands of dollars.

The Speaker's hand should be strengthened by this House in order to enable him to make such a ruling. '

dollar. In the last Ontario ' Gazette ' there were fourteen companies incorporated, two of which were mining companies. Each represented $1,000,000 capital, or $2,000,000 for both. Then, I would ask the government Minister of Mines to look into the campaign made by that well known paper ' Saturday Night ' of Toronto against wild-cat promotions. Whether it is the Toronto ' Globe ' dealing with investments in pulp, or the ' Saturday Night ' with investments in mines, or the Montreal 'Star ' with the cocaine evil, I think the members of the government should take the trouble to inquire into these grievances set forth by those or other enterprising papers, and assist in providing a remedy so far as it is in their power to do so. I cannot from my own knowledge suggest means to accomplish this, but I trust the Minister of Finance will soon be back in the House restored to health and that he will look into the matter. Then, there is another thing to which the member for Kootenay alluded and to which I may also refer.
I have thought this matter over for months, and I have been advised that were I to advocate it in the House it would be disastrous to me in my constituency, but I believe it is in the interests of Canada that attention should be called to it. There are 220 of us sitting in this Chamber legislating for a country which we know little about, What do the men in the maritime provinces know of the great west, and what do the men in the west know of the maritime provinces. Sir Oliver Mowat when premier of Ontario inaugurated expeditions through the province so that the members of the legislature might know the territory they were legislating for, and although that policy was opposed by the Conservatives then in opposition, the same system is carried out by Sir James Whitney to-day, showing that it has a useful side.
I would, therefore, ask this government once in each parliament, not once in every session but once in each parliament, to

inaugurate a system of expeditious by which the members of this parliament might learn at first hand the resources of the different portions of Canada. Commencing, say next year, let the men of the west and the men of Ontario be brought down to the maritime provinces to see the new dock yards at Halifax, to see the harbour of St. John, or the site'for the Prince Edward Island tunnel and to see the different industries and public works in that oart of the country ; and then when next year the men of the western provinces shall have seen eastern Canada, the men of eastern Canada might tire year following be taken out over the Canadian Pacific railway and brought home by the new Transcontinental railway, or the Canada Northern. I believe that if members of parliament had an opportunity in this way of seeing their country they would be better able to legislate in the interests of the whole Dominion. I do not believe that the people of Canada would in any shape or form disapprove of such a policy. It is a truism that one cannot legislate prudently and properly in reference to something he knows nothing about, and the more we know of our country the better able we are to legislate in her best interests. I might cite an example of that in my own constituency. I had been several times to the government in reference to a certain matter, and I got very scant encouragement, but the moment the minister saw the locus in quo, and saw, that in my constituency we have one of the finest ports on the Great Lakes competing only with Buffalo and United States routes, a port going through Canadian channels, which takes one-third of the grain of the west, he realized that my cause was just and that the project I was urging on him well deserved encouragement from the government of Canada. I might mention, by the way, the speech made by the hon. member for South Huron (Mr. McLean)-I think it was-which I do not think was a very patriotic speech. But, it was a speech which was not repudiated by the right hon. leader of the government. The hon. member for South Huron (Mr. McLean) said:-
But, Sir, the most silly contention I think I have ever heard made in this House is that she has protected our shores from invasion by foreign foes. Now I ask when in the memory of living man have our shores been ever threatened by a foreign foe. The only occasion I remember is what was known as the Fenian Raid, and that was not inspired by any dislike for Canada but by a dielike for Great Britain, because she denied to a certain portion of her subjects the right of privileges which _ they thought, and which I think they were justly entitled to. ' Hansard/ 1910.-p. 4419.
These, Sir, are sentiments that would not emanate from any member on this side of the House, and it is up to the member for South Huron to withdraw them. We had the other day in Ottawa, Mr. S. S. McClure, one of the most prominent newspaper and periodical publishers in the United States, and listen to his words abo.ut the British navy:-
If I were able to give you advice, which I am not, I would give you advice on the following lines. First, I would make it a matter so clear and plain that every man, woman and child should know it in his heart that the most important institution in the world to-day for human peace and justice and maintaining of the great highways of trade is the British navy.
Now, Sir, I agree with Mr. McClure, and I think I may say that the members on this side of the House agree with his words concerning the power for good of the British navy. And in one respect that is exactly where we take issue with the government of the day. In what we may call the unanimous resolution passed by the House in 1909, the principle was expressed that whatever was to be done by the Dominion of Canada must be done to strengthen the central force that went for the protection of the empire, but the naval policy placed
on the statute-books by this government has as its guiding principle that this navy of theirs is to be a separate entity, a little navy for Canada alone, which cannot go to war except an order in council is passed by the government. That is the distinction between the two parties and that is why we voted against the government Bill. Perhaps I might put that more clearly by quoting from Mr. R. T. Stead's poem, ' The Empire Builders.':-
I'st well to boast of Empire and brag of Britain's might,
I'st well to sing of her soldiers or hurry them into the fight,
I'st well to raise your anthem for the King upon his throne,
While ye leave the mother country to bear the load alone?
Many the winds that rise and fall to the flag that ye call your own,
And ye walk secure to the end6 of earth wherever that flag is known;
Safe as a child in its mother's arms ye come and ye go at will,
And ye take it all for granted

and your
mother pays the bill.
Never a wave that beats your shore but knows her floating steel,
Never a sand in your harbour fronts but knows her iron keel,
Never a child in your inland towns but lisps of her 'hearts of oak',
And the breath that ye breathe as the air of God is thick with her sulphur-smoke.
Dreaming your dreams and visions

making
your dreams come true

Offering not of your substance, offering words in lieu

Large in your little dealings, small in your great affairs,
Proud of the land that bore ye, but blind to the load she bears.
That defines the distinction between us. We on this side of the House do not propose to leave the mother country to bear the burden alone; we believe that in assisting to uphold the supremacy of the British navy we are simply assisting in the protection of our own shores.
Now, Sir, I want to say a word or two concerning certain remarks made by the hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Miller), and anything I may say will be said in a friendly manner, because the hon. gentleman and I represent adjoining constituencies and we are the best of friends. But, as I have already pointed out, whenever an hon. member on the other side of the House desires to climb up in the esteem of the Prime Minister, he proceeds forthwith to bestow on the right hon. gentleman the most fulsome eulogy, and he immediately proceeds to select a method on which to climb. And so, the hon. member for South Grey, (Mr. Miller), selected a metaphorical tree on which to climb in the estimation of the Prime Minister.

speechtext: Oh, no.

The right hon. gentleman thinks not, and I would be inclined to th'ink not also judging by the very cool manner in which my right hon. friend listened to the eulogy. I want to point out that when the hon. gentleman (Mr. Miller) selected that metaphorical tree as a means of climbing into the esteem of the Prime Minister there was some method in his madness, because as you know, if you have any suspicion that you are not going to get into office you can pluck a little graft from that tree on the way up, and then .again, if you are going to have a tumble the branches will break the fall and your friends will not hear you hit the ground. You will see, therefore, that the metaphor has its double application, and probably the hon. gentleman (Mr. Miller) selected his metaphorical tree for that reason. But, Sir, it was absolutely painful, it was cruel to see the way the hon. gentleman maltreated that tree. At one portion of the hon. genueman's peroration he took unto it wings, and I observed that the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton) who as chairman of the Conservation Commission is supposed to look after all the natural resources of this country including trees ; when he (Mr. Sifton) saw the fearful maltreatment my hon. friend (Mr. Miller) was giving to the metaphorical tree he got uneasy, and he left his seat and he walked in front of the member for South Grey (Mr. Miller) and with a strong conservation look on his,face he tried to impress upon him the advisability of leaving that tree alone, which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Miller) did forthwith. Then, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Miller) attempted to prove that because the Conservatives did not place a candidate in the field in the Drummond-Arthabaska election it was a conclusive proof that they were in alliance with the Nationalist party. Does my hon. friend (Mr. Miller) think that is a fair argument?
If he did not think so he would not have used it.

Then I ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Miller) if it is not just as fair for me to say that because Sir Wilfrid Laurier placed no candidate in the field in South York against Mr. Maclean, therefore the Prime Minister and Mr. Maclean are in an unholy alliance. I ask my hon. friend (Mr. Miller) now if that is not as fair an argument as his?
I will answer as many questions as my hon. friend chooses to put to me. I do not know that upon that occasion there was any disloyal element putting forth a candidate in South York.
The hon. gentleman is begging the question.
I say the circumstances were entirely different.

The point I am making is this : the hon. member said that because we did not put up a candidate in Drummond and Arthabaska that therefore we were in alliance with the Nationalists, and I say if his argument is good, therefore as the Liberals put up no candidate against the member for South York, would it not be as fair to say they_ were in alliance with the member for South York. Let me tell my hon. friend (Mr. Miller) that while it is quite true the Conservatives had no candidate in Drummond-Arthabaska at the last election, it is just as true that the Conservatives had no candidate in Drummond-Arthabaska at the last general election, and that, because the riding was so strongly Liberal that it was not considered advisable to put up a candidate. The argument of my hon. friend (Mr. Miller) therefore, falls to the ground because at the general election there was no question of loyalty or disloyalty, there was no question of alliance with the Nationalists because there were no Nationalists there, and yet the Conservatives had not a candidate in the field. In view of this, I think the hon. gentleman ought to admit that his assertion in that respect was absolutely unjustified. But, if the hon. gentleman will still assert that there was an alliance between the two parties, perhaps he will take the opinion of the Toronto ' Globe ' which a few days ago said :
The outstanding incident in yesterday's debate on the naval service Act of last session was Mr. Borden's assertion that the Conservatives are not in alliance with the Nationalists. That Mr. Borden's view is the correct one is shown by many indications.
I, therefore, to-day say that the assertion of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Miller) : that the Liberal-Conservatives are in alliance with the Nationalists, utterly falls to the ground, and such an assertion simply shows that these gentlemen opposite feel so keenly that public opinion is against them that they endeavour to turn the tide by making statements which they cannot substantiate by evidence. A word in conclusion-I think that any one who has listened to the speech of the leader of the opposition, having in view the fact that the unanimous resolution which was passed in this House in 1909 was not carried out by the government at all ; having in view the fact that the government came down with a mongrel navy policy to which we never assented having in view the fact that in the interval an emergency had arisen which was satisfactorily met by

the amendment of the hon. leader of the opposition, and having in view the fact that our proposition not having been carried out the two parties were at issue,
I think that no man in this country can to-day find fault with Mr. R. L. Borden's policy when he says : We are again at issue on the naval question, and we are in favour of submitting that issue to the bar of public opinion in this Dominion at the next general election.
